text:
Temperature Sensing

 Temperature Sensor Response Time and Time Constant

 A thermocouple can react in three milliseconds. The same sensor dropped into a thermowell can take over a minute.

 The sensor never changed. Everything around it did.

 
 Tau = mCp / hA 
 Live Response Calculator 
 Plunge Test vs LCSR 
 




 Temperature sensor response time and time constant describe how quickly a thermocouple or RTD's output catches up to a real process temperature change, governed by the exact same exponential math as an RC time constant circuit .


 Heat doesn't move instantly through metal. It takes real time to travel from a hot fluid, through a sheath, through any thermowell, and into the sensing element itself.


 
 
 
 That thermal lag is exactly the same phenomenon covered in this site's pressure transmitter damping guide , just driven by heat transfer instead of an electronic filter.


 
 
 Image credit: Endress+Hauser (iTHERM QuickSens Fast Response Pt100 Sensor)

 The 3 Critical Response Time Metrics

 Temperature sensors are almost always specified using one, or all three, of these standard metrics.


 
 
 t50

 Half-Time (50% Response)
 Time to reach 50% of a step temperature change, equal to 0.693 times the time constant.


 

 
 t63.2

 The Time Constant Itself
 By definition, one full time constant, the classic 63.2% point used in the plunge test standard.


 

 
 t90

 90% Response Time
 Time to reach 90% of the change, equal to 2.303 times the time constant, the figure most datasheets actually quote.


 




 Thermocouple vs RTD Response Time

 Construction differences between the two sensor types translate directly into different thermal mass.


 
 
 ⚡

 Thermocouple

 Bare wire junctions can respond in milliseconds. Sheathed, grounded junction probes are still generally faster than an equivalent RTD.

 Lower thermal mass, faster

 

 
 🌡

 RTD (Resistance Thermometer)

 The platinum element, coil former, and sheath add thermal mass, but modern thin-film designs have narrowed the gap significantly.

 Higher thermal mass, more stable

 The Thermal Time Constant Formula

 
 This formula is the thermal equivalent of an RC circuit's time constant, just built from heat transfer variables instead of electrical ones.

 
 Mass and specific heat: how much thermal energy the sensor has to absorb

 Heat transfer coefficient: how efficiently heat crosses into the sensor

 Surface area: more area exposed to flow means faster heat transfer



 
 A thicker sheath doesn't just add mass, it also changes surface area to volume ratio. Cutting sheath diameter in half can cut response time roughly in half too, for the same reason a thin wire heats up faster than a thick rod.

 Why sheath diameter dominates response time more than any other single factor






 
 Thermal Time Constant and Response Points

 τ = (ρ x V x Cp) / (h x A)

 
 Where ρ = density, V = volume, Cp = specific heat, h = heat transfer coefficient, A = surface area


 t50 = 0.693 x τ

 t63.2 = 1.000 x τ

 t90 = 2.303 x τ


 Example: τ = 10 seconds (typical thermowell installation)

 t50 = 6.93 s, t63.2 = 10 s, t90 = 23.0 s
 




 Real Response Times: Sensor to Thermowell

 Response time can vary by three orders of magnitude depending purely on installation, not sensor quality.


 
 
 Configuration Typical t63.2 / t90 
 
 
 Bare butt-welded thermocouple wire (0.001 in) t63.2 = 0.003 s 

 Fast-response RTD, direct contact (e.g. iTHERM QuickSens) t90 = 1.5 s 

 Standard sheathed RTD, direct contact t90 = 9.5 s 

 RTD in thermowell, good thermal contact t50 = 10 s, t90 = 40 s 

 RTD in thermowell with air gap t90 = 60+ s 

 
 



 Plunge Test vs LCSR: How Response Time Is Actually Measured

 Two very different methods exist, and they're used at completely different stages of a sensor's life.


 
 
 💧

 Plunge Test

 A laboratory method: the sensor is suddenly immersed in flowing water at a set velocity, and the step response is timed directly.

 Bench testing, standard reference method

 

 
 ⚡

 LCSR (Loop Current Step Response)

 An in-situ method: a current step self-heats the RTD's own element, and the heating and cooling transient reveals the actual installed response time.

 In-service testing, no removal needed

 




 LCSR testing is standard practice in nuclear power plants, where sensors can't be pulled for a plunge test without a shutdown, and validated LCSR results typically agree with plunge test values within about 10 percent.


 Where Response Time Actually Matters

 
 ⚠
 SIF and SIL Loops
 Total sensor response time eats directly into available process safety time.


 🔥
 Combustion Control
 Fast exhaust gas sensors need low thermal mass for tight control loops.


 🏭
 Food and Beverage
 Fast pasteurization verification depends on quick, repeatable response.


 ♻
 Nuclear Power
 RTD response time is a licensed technical specification, tested regularly.


 🚛
 Automotive Exhaust
 Fast RTDs track rapidly changing exhaust gas temperatures for emissions control.


 🏭
 Batch Reactors
 Slower thermowell-mounted sensors are often acceptable for large thermal mass processes.





 When the Simple Formula Breaks Down: The Biot Number

 The tau = mCp/hA formula assumes the entire sensor sits at one uniform temperature at every instant. That assumption isn't always true.

 Engineers check this with the Biot number, the ratio of internal conduction resistance to surface convection resistance. Below about 0.1, the simple lumped model holds up well.
